items.title: Instructions, overlap and evidence
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

To decode a bzip2 block, mibz2 eventually performs an odd kind of memory access. It reads an entry from a table, and the value it gets back says which entry to read next. Each 4-byte entry packs two things: its low 8 bits are one decoded byte, and the bits above them are the number of the next row to read.

let q = t[row];    // read this row's entry
row = q >> 8;      // the upper bits: the next row to read
out.push(q as u8); // the low 8 bits: one decoded byte

Suppose the walk is at row 7, and row 7's entry says that row 12 comes next. Only once that entry has arrived does the CPU know to read row 12, whose entry might point to row 4, and so on. The CPU isn't short of instructions it could run. It's short of an address. And when the entry isn't in a nearby cache, every step waits for memory.

So mibz2 doesn't walk one chain at a time. It picks about 500 starting rows spread across the table, which cuts the traversal into segments, and advances 32 of those segments in turn, so that while one lane waits for its load the others can issue theirs. In 32 lanes, 8.6 chains we measured what that buys: the 32-lane walk runs about 8.6 times as fast as a single chain.

What made it faster? It's tempting to say we'd found how many memory requests the CPU can keep in flight at once, its memory-level parallelism (MLP). But the same change also handed the CPU's scheduler far more independent instructions, which is instruction-level parallelism (ILP). Which of the two explains the speedup, and does the answer change what we should try to make faster?

The same question came up in 2022, in replies to Daniel Lemire's post Memory-level parallelism: Intel Ice Lake versus Amazon Graviton 3. Lemire measures MLP with a benchmark much like our walk: a long pointer chase through a large array, then the same accesses shared among more and more independent chains. Ivica Bogosavljevic replied that the speedup comes from ILP as well; Lemire, that the waits are memory loads, not instructions.

They were both right, because ILP and MLP aren't rival explanations here: the independent instructions are what let the memory requests overlap, so the two names describe one mechanism from its two ends. The more useful question is what a speedup like our 8.6 can tell you about the part of the machine that limits it. It shows that overlapping the chains pays, but not what stops the gain from growing, and so not what to make faster next. We found that out on our own walk: removing a third of its instructions made it about 12% faster on its own, and left the decoder no faster with four workers.

The sections below take that argument in order: why one chain stalls; how ILP and MLP fit together; what Lemire's curve can and can't measure; what happened when we cut the walk's instructions; and where the four-worker decoder's extra time goes instead.

items.title: Memory-level parallelism in mibz2: instructions, overlap and evidence
items.text:
Interleaving pointer chases lets memory waits overlap. The speedup shows that this pays, but not what limits it: a 2022 exchange about Daniel Lemire's benchmark, read against mibz2's inverse-BWT walk.

2 November 2026 · 15 min read · Research synthesis

items.title: 1. Why a pointer chase stalls
items.text:
Stripped of the decoding, the walk is the classic pointer chase. Written in C, with next standing for the table, each step is

p = next[p];

and the value each load returns is the address of the next. An out-of-order CPU looks far ahead in the instruction stream for work it can start early, but it can't issue a load whose address it doesn't know yet, and no amount of lookahead can supply a value that hasn't arrived.

Unrolling the loop, writing the step out four times, doesn't change that:

p = next[p];
p = next[p];
p = next[p];
p = next[p];

That saves a little loop bookkeeping, but the four loads are still one chain, each waiting for the last. What does help is giving the loop four independent chains:

p0 = next[p0];
p1 = next[p1];
p2 = next[p2];
p3 = next[p3];

Each lane still waits on itself from one round to the next. Within a round, though, all four addresses are known, so all four loads can be issued without waiting for one another.

Unrolling one chain, and interleaving four

One chain, unrolled four timesp = next[p]p = next[p]p = next[p]p = next[p]Each load’s address is the value the load before it returned.Four chains, interleavedround 1round 2round 3lane 0p0 = next[p0]p0 = next[p0]p0 = next[p0]…lane 1p1 = next[p1]p1 = next[p1]p1 = next[p1]…lane 2p2 = next[p2]p2 = next[p2]p2 = next[p2]…lane 3p3 = next[p3]p3 = next[p3]p3 = next[p3]…Arrows join each lane’s rounds. No arrow joins one lane to another, so a round’s four addresses are known together. Arrows mean "needs the result of". Unrolling lays one chain's loads out in the source, but each still waits for the last. Interleaving gives every round four loads whose addresses are known together. Whether they actually overlap is up to the processor and the memory system.

Nothing here needs real pointers. A chain of integer indices behaves the same way, and the lanes can share one array. mibz2's table of row numbers is exactly this kind of chain.

items.title: Faster, without any load getting quicker
items.text:
Suppose, with made-up round numbers, that each dependent load takes 80 ns to come back from memory. One chain then completes 12.5 million steps a second. If eight chains overlap perfectly, eight loads are in flight at once and the walk completes 100 million steps a second: one every 10 ns on average, even though each load still takes 80 ns.

That changes how busy the CPU looks. A common measure of busyness is instructions per cycle (IPC): how many instructions the processor completes, on average, in one tick of its clock. A modern core can complete several per cycle when it has independent work and its data close at hand. An IPC of 1 means one instruction per cycle; an IPC of 0.1 means one every ten cycles. A core that spends most of its time waiting for memory has a low IPC, even when it's doing exactly what we want.

In the example, at 3 GHz an 80 ns wait is 240 cycles. If each step runs three instructions, one chain completes three instructions every 240 cycles:

\[ \mathrm{IPC}_{\text{1 chain}} \approx \frac{3}{240} = 0.0125 \]

With eight chains overlapping, eight steps' worth complete in the same 240 cycles, an IPC of about 0.1. The walk is eight times faster, and the CPU still completes only one instruction every ten cycles.

That's the situation Lemire described when he replied that IPC in his benchmark is "small (much less than one)". A low IPC fits a loop that mostly waits for memory, and it shows that a large speedup doesn't need the core to look any busier. It doesn't say which part of the machine the loop is waiting on, and it doesn't show that the extra independent instructions played no part. That's the other half of the argument.

items.title: 2. ILP exposes the work; MLP lets it overlap
items.text:
Ivica's objection was that the interleaved loop isn't only demonstrating memory-level parallelism:

Ivica Bogosavljevic's reply to Lemire's post, 8 June 2022. Read the whole exchange

Ivica Bogosavljevic, 8 June 2022: I read the post, the overall idea of the post is good, but I think it misses a few important things to make the whole picture more clear:

Ivica Bogosavljevic, 8 June 2022: (1) You use the term memory-level parallelism, but the speedup you are getting are not only because of it, but because of instruction-level parallelism. When you interleaved additional work, you broke some hard instruction dependencies, …

Ivica Bogosavljevic, 8 June 2022: … increased ILP so an out-of-order CPU had more available ILP and could run more instructions per cycle. You wouldn't achieve the same thing on an in-order CPU.

Ivica Bogosavljevic, 8 June 2022: (2) You should have measured instruction per cycle or cycle per instruction metric to measure CPU efficiency. Also you should have measured instruction count as well.

Ivica Bogosavljevic, 8 June 2022: (3) The data structure is a linked list, but it is not clear how it was allocated. Are loads mostly hitting L1, L2 or LL cache?

Denis Yaroshevskiy, 9 June 2022: Following of this - how big is the read and does it matter how big is the read.

Daniel Lemire, 9 June 2022, 1:58: This is out of cache and the instructions per cycle is small (much less than one). Obviously it assumes a superscalar processor but that's a prerequisite for a core to have multiple loads in flight. The source code is fully available. 1/2

Daniel Lemire, 9 June 2022: The approach is now pretty much standard and is used by many people. I am certainly happy to receive criticism. If you have a reasonable alternative measure of a core's memory-level parallelism, please share. 2/2

Daniel Lemire, 9 June 2022: Note that the hard dependencies are memory loads… not instructions… the instructions are mostly just out-of-cache memory loads. Please refer to the post for link to source code.

Both of them are describing the same event from different ends. In the interleaved loop:

  1. the program exposes independent load instructions;
  2. the processor issues them before the earlier ones finish;
  3. their memory requests overlap;
  4. more steps complete per second.

The first two steps are ILP and the last two are MLP: the opportunity, and what the memory system makes of it. They aren't two separate speedups to be added up. The independence of the instructions is what lets the memory requests overlap. Work on MLP treats them together for that reason: how far ahead the instruction window reaches, and how scheduling and branches behave, decide how much memory concurrency a core can actually achieve (Chou, Fahs and Abraham, ISCA 2004).

Each side's wording is a little loose. Interleaving doesn't "break" any dependency, as Ivica put it: each chain keeps all of its own, and independent chains are added alongside. And loads are instructions, so "memory loads, not instructions" really means that the delay on the critical path is the memory system's, not arithmetic's. Neither claim about processors is universal either. A core doesn't have to be superscalar or out of order to keep several misses in flight: Berkeley's single-issue, in-order Rocket core has a nonblocking data cache, and Arm documents three outstanding misses, under some conditions, on the in-order Cortex-A55 (the appendix has the sources). An in-order core is simply much more sensitive to the order in which the loads appear.

Ivica's request for instruction counts and IPC is still a good one, and he has since shown interleaved code that executes more instructions and runs faster (Johnny's Software Lab). His point isn't that instructions must be minimised. It's that once the loads are exposed, something decides how fast they complete, and the speedup curve alone doesn't say what.

items.title: 3. What Lemire's speedup really measures
items.text:
Lemire's benchmark is a careful version of the loop above (source, as published before the 2022 post). It fills a 256 MiB array of 64-bit indices with a random permutation that forms one long cycle, starts each lane at a different point on the cycle, and keeps the total number of accesses fixed as lanes are added, so more lanes reschedule the same work rather than doing more of it. The 2022 post reports about 90 ns for a single lane on the Ice Lake machine and 120 ns on Graviton 3, and describes the two as sustaining about 25 and 19 loads at once.

Figures like those come from where the curve stops rising; the benchmark's code, for instance, reports the lane count at which one more lane improves the time by less than 1%. A plateau like that can have many causes:

  • the core runs out of slots for outstanding misses;
  • the instruction window fills before it reaches more loads;
  • address generation or load throughput saturates;
  • the TLB and page walker can't keep up;
  • registers spill as lanes are added;
  • requests take longer once many are queued;
  • bandwidth runs out;
  • or noise lands near the 1% threshold.

The curve alone can't tell these apart. So "about 25 loads at once" is safest read as a statement about the whole machine running this workload: around the 25th lane, another chain stopped buying more overlap. It needn't be the size of any one queue. As Travis Downs pointed out in an earlier discussion of the same benchmark, every queue between the core and DRAM affects the plateau, and what matters is not only how many entries a queue has but how long each request holds one. Changing the page size moved the plateau too. A 256 MiB array spans 65,536 pages of 4 KiB, so translation is part of what the benchmark measures.

items.title: How big is the read?
items.text: Denis Yaroshevskiy's question, how big each read is and whether it matters, turns out to go to the heart of the bandwidth figures. Each load reads 8 bytes, but the program reports bandwidth by counting 64 bytes per access, one cache line. That's a model of the traffic, not a measurement of it: a line may already be cached, two accesses may share a line, prefetches add traffic of their own, and page walks add more. The size of an instruction's operand, the line it pulls in, the useful bytes it delivers and the page it translates through are four different things. That distinction matters for mibz2, whose table entries are 4 bytes.

items.title: Four things called MLP
items.text:
By this point "memory-level parallelism" has been used for at least four different quantities:

Quantity The question it answers Independence in the software How many chains can advance at once? Capacity in the hardware How many entries does a particular queue have? Achieved occupancy How many requests are outstanding, on average? Speedup, or the knee of the curve How much faster is it, and when does another lane stop helping?

They needn't agree. A program can run 32 lanes and keep eight requests outstanding. An eightfold speedup doesn't prove that eight DRAM requests were in flight on average. And occupancy can rise for a bad reason as well as a good one: if each request takes longer to complete, more of them are outstanding at any moment even though no more work gets done.

None of this makes the benchmark wrong. It's a sound, open way to show that overlapping dependent chains pays, which is what Lemire defended. What its curve can't do is name the resource that stops it rising. That gap matters as soon as you try to make such a loop faster by changing its instructions, which is what we did next.

items.title: 4. Cutting instructions helped the walk, but not four-worker throughput
items.text:
In the version of mibz2 examined here, the inverse-BWT walk runs 32 lanes over up to 512 segments. Each ordinary step is close to the loop we started with, plus a prefetch:

let q = t[lane.row];
lane.row = q >> 8;
prefetch(t, lane.row);
output_for_lane[offset] = q as u8;

As soon as a lane's entry arrives, its next row is known, and the walk asks for it straight away. It then serves the other lanes before coming back.

The prefetch's lead time in the 32-lane walk

lane 0q = t[row]row = q >> 8prefetch(t, row)out[i] = q as u8lane 1its ownsteplane 2its ownsteplane 3its ownsteplane 0 againq = t[row]the prefetched rowthe prefetch’s lead time: the work on lanes 1 to 3order of execution, not to scale Four of the 32 lanes, in execution order, with no durations. The work on the other lanes is the time the prefetch has to arrive. If it's shorter than the memory latency, lane 0's next load still waits. A prefetch can't reach a second hop: that address isn't known until the next entry arrives.

Our table is also much smaller than Lemire's array. A full block of 900,000 rows of 4-byte entries is 3.6 MB, against his 256 MiB. That's far bigger than a core's private L2 but small enough to fit, on its own, in the 20 MiB shared L3 of the workstation we test on. Fitting isn't the same as hitting: capacity alone doesn't tell us how often its accesses are served from L3 while four workers decode at once.

The 8.6 from the introduction is the ratio of two measured costs, 38.55 cycles per byte for one chain and 4.49 for the 32-lane walk. It's a throughput factor, not a count of requests in flight. All 32 lanes can do useful work even if only some have a request outstanding at any instant.

items.title: When instructions become the limit
items.text:
A rough model shows why instructions might matter once the lanes are there. The time per step can't be shorter than the slowest of three limits:

\[ c_{\text{step}} \gtrsim \max\left( \frac{L}{K},\ \frac{u}{P},\ \frac{b}{B} \right) \]

Here \(L/K\) is the memory latency shared among \(K\) independent chains, \(u/P\) the instruction work per step over the rate the core can execute it, and \(b/B\) the bytes per step over the available bandwidth. It's optimistic and leaves a great deal out, but it captures the turn in the story, because shrinking one term helps only while that term is the largest. With one chain, \(L/K\) dominates and trimming instructions barely helps. Add enough chains and \(L/K\) falls until the instruction work, or the traffic, takes over. At that point fewer instructions should mean a faster walk: they shorten the work per step, they free load and address-generation slots, and they let the instruction window reach more loads.

So we tried it. An experiment unrolled all 32 lane steps so that each used fixed offsets, removing most of the walk's bookkeeping (assembly comparison):

Per ordinary lane step, hot loop Original Unrolled Instructions 16.4 10.44 Loads 3.0 3.06 Stores 2.03 2.16 Prefetches 1 1

About 36% of the instructions went, while the memory operations stayed. On its own, on an EPYC 7763, the unrolled walk took 0.877 of the original's time (95% interval 0.863 to 0.891): about 12% less.

Then it went into the whole decoder, in a registered trial on our test workstation (results):

Decoder throughput, unrolled ÷ original Point 95% interval One worker 1.017 1.006–1.028 Four workers 1.000 0.987–1.012

With four workers, the configuration that matters, the gain was nothing. A control workload's CPU cost got worse, and the trial's verdict was negative.

The two results come from different processors, so together they don't isolate one cause. A plausible reading is that the removed instructions weren't using the resource that limits the four-worker decoder: the archive's own explanation, pressure on the workstation's load and address ports, comes from a static model, not a measurement. What the pair does establish is the point of Ivica's objection. Cutting instructions can make a loop faster in isolation and make no difference to the program it lives in.

For optimisation, a bottleneck is the resource whose relief improves the figure you care about. The walk's extra instructions were real work, but removing them didn't improve four-worker throughput, so for that figure they weren't the bottleneck. In the model's terms, the instruction term \(u/P\) wasn't the largest one when four workers shared the machine, and shrinking a term that isn't the largest changes nothing.

items.title: 5. The bottleneck isn't an instruction count
items.text:
If not instructions, then what? Our earlier attribution of the whole decoder (analysis) compared one worker with four:

Per decoded byte One worker Four workers Instructions retired 32.63 33.06 CPU cycles 13.46 17.51 IPC 2.42 1.89

With four workers the decoder retires almost exactly the same instructions per byte (1.3% more) but needs 30% more cycles to complete them. Note too that IPC is above one in both columns, so "IPC below one means memory-bound" wouldn't have classified this workload either way. IPC is a ratio of two things that can each change, and a change that cuts instructions can lower IPC and still save cycles.

Much of that extra time is in the inverse-BWT step. On 197 matched full-sized blocks, traversal plus assembly rises from 1.234 to 1.806 CPU ns per row with four workers (corrected proposal). Four full tables take 14.4 MB of the workstation's 20 MiB L3 before any other buffer, so the workers are plausibly competing for cache and for the path to memory, but the arithmetic alone doesn't prove it. The previous post describes the experiments designed to test it.

items.title: Counters can mislead in the same way
items.text:
Hardware counters are the obvious way to find out, but they need the same care as Lemire's curve. Intel defines an "MLP" metric as the number of pending L1 demand misses summed over cycles, divided by the number of cycles in which any such miss was pending. Between one worker and four, that figure hardly changed, staying near 2.18. That sounds like nothing changed. But the share of cycles with a miss pending rose from about 12% to about 30%, so averaged over all cycles the occupancy rose from roughly \(2.18 \times 0.12 \approx 0.26\) to \(2.18 \times 0.30 \approx 0.65\). The metric was answering a narrower question than its name suggests.

One occupancy trace, three ratios

cycle 0cycle 1cycle 2cycle 3cycle 4cycle 5request Aoutstanding 3 cyclesrequest Boutstanding 3 cyclesoutstanding012210O = 6 request-cyclesA = 2 requestsP = 4 pending cyclesC = 6 cyclesO ÷ A = 3 cycles per requesthow long a request stays outstandingO ÷ P = 1.5 requestsoccupancy while anything is pendingO ÷ C = 1.0 requestoccupancy over the whole window A made-up trace, not mibz2 data. Dividing the same total by requests, by busy cycles or by all cycles gives three different answers: how long requests last, how many overlap while any are pending, and how many are pending on average.

The same caution applies to every counter we read: what it counts, over which cycles, for which requests. The technical appendix goes through the counters behind these figures, two earlier readings of them that we've withdrawn, and the measurements that would separate the remaining explanations.

items.title: Exposing work isn't the same as completing it
items.text:
Put together, the argument runs:

  1. A dependent pointer chase waits on memory at every step, because each load's address is the value the previous load returned.
  2. Independent chains give the processor loads it can issue together (ILP), and their requests overlap in the memory system (MLP). Throughput rises though no load gets faster.
  3. The speedup, and the lane count where it levels off, show that the overlap pays. They don't show which resource stops it, because many different limits produce the same curve.
  4. So a cost that looks large isn't necessarily the one to cut. Removing a third of mibz2's walk instructions made the walk faster on its own and left the four-worker decoder where it was. Four workers retire the same instructions per byte as one, and take longer to complete them.

So the next gain won't come from counting instructions, or from counting requests in flight. It will come from finding which resource the traversal is actually waiting on when four workers share the machine, and changing whatever consumes it.

items.title: BWT space–time tradeoff
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

In 2001, Julian Seward, the author of bzip2 and the original designer of Valgrind, was working at Microsoft Research in Cambridge. That year he presented a paper at the IEEE Data Compression Conference, Space-time tradeoffs in the Inverse B-W Transform, on what it costs to undo the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT) that bzip2 is built on.

Compression with the BWT had been studied closely, but "decompression-time issues remain underinvestigated". He had two uses in mind that pull in opposite directions: booting a Linux kernel from a compressed image needs little memory, and an on-the-fly disk compressor needs speed. So he offers a family of algorithms that trade one for the other. At one extreme, the BWT can be inverted, slowly, in one byte of memory per byte of block. At the other:

we argue that the maximum speed of BWT decompression is unavoidably constrained by the rate at which cache misses are serviced.

mibz2 is our bzip2 decoder, written for the Wikidata dumps, and that sentence could stand over most of what we have written about it. Our posts on 32 lanes and memory-level parallelism are about keeping many misses in flight at once; memory interference is about four workers' misses competing for one memory system; compact navigation tables is about taking fewer misses with a smaller table. Seward said as much in bzip2's manual: "performance, both for compressing and decompressing, is largely determined by the speed at which your machine can service cache misses."

The post has two halves: how Seward's algorithms work and what he measured, then what happens to his tradeoff in mibz2, where several blocks decode at once and share one cache. The result in the second half is a controlled test of the walk alone, not yet of the whole decoder.

Seward's paper, 2001

  1. 1How does a decoder get banana back?By a chain of table lookups, each depending on the last
  2. 2Making inversion fastbasis, bw94 and mergedTL: byte and link in one word
  3. 3Spending less memoryindexF and the count trees: recompute instead of store
  4. 4What Seward measuredMemory against speed: the space–time tradeoff

mibz2, 2026

  1. 5Four blocks, one cacheWhy the tradeoff changes when blocks decode at once
  2. 6A smaller table, a busier lookupA little over half the space, more work per lookup
  3. 7The four-worker reversalThe walk alone: slower on one core, faster on four
  4. 8Why four workers cost moreThe usual table pays far more for sharing the cache
  5. 9Still to buildA cheap way to construct the table for the decoder

items.title: Revisiting the space–⁠time tradeoff in BWT inversion
items.text:
In 2001, Seward showed why the fastest way to undo a Burrows–Wheeler transform could use more instructions but less memory traffic. Twenty-five years later, that observation led us to ask whether a smaller navigation table could do more work per step and still come out ahead under contention. A first measurement of ours shows it doing so.

2 November 2026 · 23 min read · Result

items.title: 1. From sorted rotations to the transformation vector
items.text:
Start with the word banana and see what the Burrows–Wheeler transform does to it.

First, write out six versions of the word, each starting at a different letter and wrapping round to the beginning when it reaches the end: banana, ananab, nanaba, anaban, nabana, abanan. These are the word's cyclic rotations: the same six letters, each time in a different order. Then sort the six rotations alphabetically and stack them as rows:

The six rotations of banana, sorted

row first last 0 a b a n a n 1 a n a b a n 2 a n a n a b 3 b a n a n a 4 n a b a n a 5 n a n a b a the original word nnbaaa, read down The transform keeps the last column, nnbaaa, and the number of the row holding banana, 3. Nothing else of the square is stored. The rotations of banana in alphabetical order. The first column is shaded green and the last blue; row 3, outlined, is banana itself.

Read down the last column of the sorted rows, and it spells nnbaaa. The original banana is in row 3, counting from zero. The transform keeps just those two things, the last column and the row number, and stores nothing else. It doesn't make the block smaller; the reordered letters compress better in bzip2's later stages, for a reason that comes below.

How can a decoder get banana back from only nnbaaa and 3? Each of Seward's algorithms answers that question in a different way.

Seward names the pieces with letters, following Burrows and Wheeler's 1994 report A Block-sorting Lossless Data Compression Algorithm. On the same square:

Seward's names for the pieces

0 a b a n a n 1 a n a b a n 2 a n a n a b 3 b a n a n a 4 n a b a n a 5 n a n a b a F first column: aaabnn L last column: nnbaaa M every rotation of S, sorted: N × N letters, N = 6 S the block: banana I its row: 3 Stored by bzip2: L and I. Everything else here, the decoder has to work out. The square of sorted rotations again, with each symbol pointing at what it names. In bzip2, N can be up to 900,000.

Decoding builds two more things of its own, which the rest of this section explains: \(C\), a count of each letter, and \(T\), which Seward calls the "transformation vector". The decoder's whole path, from what is stored back to the word:

What the decoder rebuilds

L nnbaaa C a3 b1 n2 F aaabnn T 4 5 3 0 1 2 S banana count expand match walk L is used again to match each byte to its occurrence in F; the walk starts at row I = 3 Each arrow is a step explained in the rest of this section: counting, expanding the counts into F, matching occurrences to get T, and the walk.

So the decoder is given \(L\) and \(I\) and must produce \(S\). It never holds \(M\): the inverse transform recovers just enough of it, from \(L\), to read off row \(I\).

Why the first and last columns. Every row of \(M\) is \(S\) read round from some starting point, so in every row the last byte comes just before the first, going round \(S\). Row 3 ends in a and starts with b, and the final a of banana comes, going round, before its opening b. That is the relation the whole paper builds on: \(L[i]\) comes just before \(F[i]\) in \(S\). The two columns carry different information:

  • \(F\) is the bytes of \(S\) in sorted order, so the counts alone fix it. A decoder holding \(L\) can rebuild \(F\) by counting, so it is never sent.
  • \(L\) holds the byte that precedes each row's opening context, with the rows sorted by context. Bytes before similar contexts tend to repeat (in English, he is often preceded by t), so \(L\) has long runs, which bzip2's later stages compress.

So a bzip2 block carries \(L\), with \(I\) to say which row is \(S\), and the decoder rebuilds the order of \(S\) from them with \(T\).

Defining \(T\). Seward's theory section is "a more detailed exposition of Algorithm D in §2 of [1]", Burrows and Wheeler's decompression algorithm, because "the increased detail exposes a range of possible implementations". Everything rests on "establishing the relationship between the \(F\) and \(L\) vectors, and recording this in the 'transformation vector' \(T\)":

\[ M[j, N-1]\; M[j, 0..N-2] = M[i, 0..N-1] \quad\Longrightarrow\quad T[j] = i. \]

Take row \(j\) and move its last byte to the front. That is another rotation of \(S\), so it is some row \(i\) of \(M\), and \(T[j]\) records which. Row 0, abanan, becomes nabana, row 4, so \(T[0] = 4\). Moving the last byte to the front starts the string one byte earlier in \(S\), so following \(T\) walks \(S\) backwards.

Walking \(T\). Row \(T[j]\) starts with the byte row \(j\) ends with, which comes just before row \(j\)'s first byte in \(S\). So \(F[T[i]]\) precedes \(F[i]\). The decoder has \(L\), not \(F\), but \(L[k] = F[T[k]]\), and substituting gives a relation in \(L\) alone:

\[ L[T[k]] \text{ immediately precedes } L[k] \text{ in } S. \]

\(L[I]\) is the last byte of \(S\), so starting at \(I\) and following \(T\) gives \(S\) from the end:

Decoding banana by following T

row visited byte read 3 a → 0 n → 4 a → 1 n → 5 a → 2 b j L[j] T[j] 0 n 4 1 n 5 2 b 3 3 a 0 4 a 1 5 a 2 S, written from the end 0 1 2 3 4 5 a Step 1: row 3, emit L[3] = a into S[5]; next row T[3] = 0 n Step 2: row 0, emit L[0] = n into S[4]; next row T[0] = 4 a Step 3: row 4, emit L[4] = a into S[3]; next row T[4] = 1 n Step 4: row 1, emit L[1] = n into S[2]; next row T[1] = 5 a Step 5: row 5, emit L[5] = a into S[1]; next row T[5] = 2 b Step 6: row 2, emit L[2] = b into S[0]; done S = banana, recovered by following T from row I = 3 Across the top, the rows the walk visits and the byte it reads at each. Below, each step reads the byte in L at the current row, writes it into S from the end, and moves to the row T names. Every jump depends on the entry just read, which is why the walk is one dependent load after another.

That is banana backwards, and it is the whole inner loop of the inverse transform: load the entry at \(p\), emit a byte, jump where it says. Where each jump lands depends on the content of \(S\), not on the last jump. In a million-byte block that is a million loads from places the cache has no reason to hold.

To write \(S\) forwards, Seward assumes the compressor reverses each block before sorting. bzip2 doesn't, which a footnote calls "a design flaw"; by the manual's account, "the bzip2 format was frozen before I properly and fully understood the performance consequences". Its decoder builds the links the other way instead, writing \(i\) into slot \(s\) where Seward would set \(T[i] = s\) (tt[cftab[uc]++] |= i << 8), and following that \(T^{-1}\) emits \(S\) forwards. mibz2 does the same, so its navigation table holds \(T^{-1}\): each entry points forwards, to the row whose string starts one byte later in \(S\).

Building \(T\) from counts. The rows of \(M\) are sorted, and two rows ending in the same byte keep their order when that byte moves to the front, since the rest of each row decides it. So the \(k\)-th \(c\) in \(L\) rotates into the \(k\)-th row starting with \(c\): "if \(c\) occurs \(k\) times in \(L[0..j]\) and \(L[j] = c\), then \(T[j]\) must be \(i\), where \(i\) is the position of the \(k\)-th \(c\) in \(F\)."

T matches each L byte to the same occurrence in F

L[j] F[i] j = 0 n a i = 0 j = 1 n a i = 1 j = 2 b a i = 2 j = 3 a b i = 3 j = 4 a n i = 4 j = 5 a n i = 5 T[0] = 4 T[1] = 5 T[2] = 3 T[3] = 0 T[4] = 1 T[5] = 2 The k-th a in L is the k-th a in F, and so for every byte: the links never cross within one byte. The k-th a in L goes to the k-th a in F, and likewise for n and b: T = 4 5 3 0 1 2, from counts and one scan.

The \(c\)'s in \(F\) form one bucket. Turning the counts in \(C\) into running totals gives where each bucket starts: \(C[c]\) becomes the number of bytes smaller than \(c\) (for banana, a 0, b 3, n 4). So

\[ T[j] = C[c] + k - 1, \qquad c = L[j], \]

and one scan of \(L\) with a running count per byte value builds \(T\). Within each byte value the links increase with \(j\). Every BWT has this ordering, and our compact table depends on it.

items.title: 2. Making inversion fast: basis, bw94 and mergedTL
items.text:
"How fast can inversion be?" Three algorithms, each refining the last, answer it.

basis is the theory written out: count, build \(T\), walk. It reads \(L\) three times and keeps \(L\) (one byte a row) and \(T\) (four) alive: \(5N\) bytes.

bw94, named for Burrows and Wheeler's report, merges the first two passes by recording \(T'[i]\), the number of earlier occurrences of \(L[i]\), while counting. That is \(T\) without its bucket's start, \(T[i] = T'[i] + C[L[i]]\), and the walk adds the start back. Two passes, still \(5N\) bytes.

mergedTL comes from looking at bw94's walk, which reads \(L[p]\) and \(T'[p]\) at the same arbitrary index: "Unless both \(T\) and \(L\) fit in the machine's cache, this could cause two (capacity) misses per iteration." So it packs both into one 32-bit word, limiting \(N\) to \(2^{24}\):

\[ U[i] = 256 \cdot T'[i] + L[i]. \]

The name is literal: \(T\) and \(L\), merged. Each step unpacks the byte with a mask and the link with a shift, which costs instructions, "but the near-halving of the cache miss rate is potentially valuable". The table is also a byte a row smaller: \(4N\).

What one row costs, bit by bit

0 bits 8 16 24 32 bits bw94 T′[i] T′[i], displacement in its bucket array 1 L[i] L[i] array 2: a second line mergedTL U[i] T′[i], 24 bits L[i] one word: U = 256·T′ + L indexF A[i] low 16 bits of T[i] 4 byte: binary search in C bzip2, mibz2 tt[s] i such that T[i] = s, 24 bits L[s] the link reversed indexF's 20 bits sit in two arrays: 16 in one, and a 4-bit nibble packed two to a byte in another. bw94 keeps T′ and L in separate arrays, so a step can miss twice. mergedTL packs both into one word. indexF keeps only T, in 20 bits, and finds the byte from the counts. bzip2 and mibz2 pack the byte with the reversed link.

bzip2 uses mergedTL, with the reversed link stored as an absolute position, so its walk needs no \(C[c]\) addition. Its manual credits the change with a real gain: "Single array implementation of the inverse BWT. This significantly speeds up decompression, presumably because it reduces the number of cache misses."

items.title: 3. Spending less memory: indexF and the trees
items.text:
"Can we reduce memory use whilst retaining useful decompression speed? Interestingly, yes." The relation in \(F\), \(F[T[i]]\) precedes \(F[i]\), needs only \(T\) to walk. If the decoder reads the output bytes from \(F\) instead of \(L\), it needs \(L\) only while it builds \(T\), so \(T\) can be written over it. \(F\) needn't be stored either: it is sorted, so the 256 running totals in \(C\) describe it, and \(F[p]\) is the byte whose bucket contains \(p\). "No free lunch, alas": finding it is a binary search in \(C\).

indexF, named for indexing into \(F\), keeps \(T\) alone in \(N\) 20-bit words (so \(N \le 2^{20}\)): a 16-bit array plus a nibble array, \(2.5N\) bytes. It starts the walk at \(T[I]\), because reading \(F\), the byte \(L[I]\) is found at \(F[T[I]]\). bzip2 ships it as -s, "a modified algorithm which only requires 2.5 bytes per block byte … albeit at about half the normal speed", with the search as BZ2_indexIntoF. What it gives up:

  • A search per byte, eight or nine comparisons where mergedTL has a mask. The 1 KB of counts stays in cache, so the search costs instructions, not misses, and since the next position is \(A[p]\) alone, a processor can overlap it with the next load.
  • Two arrays again. The 20-bit entry is split between the 16-bit array and the nibbles, so a step can touch two cache lines, the cost mergedTL removed.
  • A cap of \(2^{20}\) bytes per block, which bzip2's 900,000-byte maximum fits.

The trees. "It is instructive to ask just how little storage we can get away with": \(L\) and the counts alone. Any \(T[j]\) is \(C[c]\) plus the number of \(c\)'s before \(j\) in \(L\), but counting them means scanning \(L\), \(O(N)\) a step and \(O(N^2)\) in all: "absurdly inefficient". Seward buys speed back with 256 binary trees of partial counts, one per byte value. Each node counts its byte in an aligned power-of-two segment of \(L\), an empty subtree costs nothing, and a node budget sets how deep the trees grow. To count the \(c\)'s up to \(j\), descend \(c\)'s tree, adding the left child's count whenever \(j\) lies to the right, and scan \(L\) only for the last segment.

A count tree answers a rank query

[0, 8) · 3 [0, 4) · 1 [4, 8) · 2 [2, 4) · 1 [4, 6) · 2 [0, 2) · none [6, 8) · none n 0 n 1 b 2 a 3 a 4 a 5 6 7 L padding How many a's in L[0..4]? Right at the root (+1 from [0, 4)), left to [4, 6), off the tree: scan L[4..4] (+1). Two. The tree for byte a over L = nnbaaa, padded to 8 positions. Counting the a's up to position 4 takes one left-child count and a one-byte scan, so T[4] = C[a] + 2 − 1 = 1.

tree stores a node in three 32-bit words. treeopt packs a node into 54 bits, two words, and a leaf into one, fitting nearly twice as many nodes in the same space, which halves the scans. With \(L\), tree-1M and treeopt-1M take \(2N\) bytes and treeopt-500k \(1.5N\).

items.title: 4. What Seward measured
items.text:
The machine was a 400 MHz AMD K6-III with 128 MB of memory and a 256 KB second-level cache. Each block, at most 10⁶ bytes, was inverted ten times. How much memory each algorithm needs for a 10⁶-byte block:

Algorithm Memory Seward's description basis 5000 kB Straightforward derivation from theory bw94 5000 kB As per [1], does 2 passes, not 3 mergedTL 4000 kB As bw94 but more cache-friendly indexF 2500 kB Indexes into \(F\) rather than \(L\) tree-1M 2000 kB Computes \(T\) incrementally; 1 megabyte extra space treeopt-1M 2000 kB More space-economical version of tree-1M treeopt-500k 1500 kB As treeopt-1M but with only 500k auxiliary space

He tested them on six files of at least a megabyte, four from the Canterbury Corpus. The last column names the nearest of mibz2's benchmark corpora, loosely:

File kB What it is Nearest in mibz2's corpora bible 4047.4 The King James Bible text, though ours is source code, repeated world192 2473.4 The CIA World Factbook, 1992 none: Wikidata's subject matter, not its format ecoli 4638.7 The E. coli genome, in four letters none kennedy 1029.7 An Excel spreadsheet runs, and at the extreme onebyte netscape 7678.8 Netscape Navigator 4.75, an x86 executable records, binary bashtgz 1708.8 bash 2.04's source, gzipped random

How fast each algorithm inverted each file, in MB/s, with the fastest in bold. mergedTL is the fastest on every one:

bashtgz bible ecoli kennedy netscape world192 Mean basis 1.54 1.72 1.53 2.46 2.32 1.65 1.86 bw94 1.58 1.77 1.57 2.54 2.41 1.69 1.93 mergedTL 2.49 2.76 2.48 4.72 3.51 2.65 3.10 indexF 1.20 1.36 1.30 1.71 1.67 1.31 1.43 tree-1M 0.032 0.211 0.325 0.099 0.044 0.207 0.153 treeopt-1M 0.059 0.301 0.342 0.167 0.099 0.298 0.211 treeopt-500k 0.032 0.218 0.339 0.100 0.036 0.198 0.154

The paper gives these numbers only as tables. Plotting each algorithm's average speed against its memory shows the space–time tradeoff between them:

Seward's measured speed–memory choices

0 1 2 3 1 2 3 4 5 working memory, MB for a 10⁶-byte block (Table 1) average rate, MB/s (Table 3) mergedTL 3.10 indexF 1.43 bw94 1.93 basis 1.86 the three tree variants, 0.15–0.21 Each algorithm's average rate over the six files against its memory, from Seward's Tables 1 and 3, on a 400 MHz K6-III in 2001. The paper gives the numbers as tables; the plot is ours.

It isn't a smooth curve on which each saved byte costs speed. mergedTL is "on average 61% and 67% faster than bw94 and basis respectively, at the same time using less memory": it beats both on both axes, by changing how the next link is read. indexF runs at 46% of its speed in 62.5% of its memory. Below that, half a byte a row less costs a factor of seven.

Seward then asks why. Simulating the K6-III's cache with cacheprof, his own profiler, he counted per byte of bible:

instructions memory references misses bw94 18.00 9.00 1.63 mergedTL 20.00 8.00 0.88

mergedTL runs 11% more instructions and takes 54% as many misses. 89.4% of those misses are the walk's reads of \(U[p]\), and 78.6% of those reads miss, because \(T\) holds "a completely arbitrary permutation" that the decoder "is obliged to traverse". So "there appears to be no way to avoid a miss rate approaching one per \(L\)-byte", and mergedTL is "a realistic upper bound on inversion performance".

kennedy inverts nearly twice as fast as bashtgz because its long runs make \(T\) point each row at its neighbour, which is usually already cached; random input sets the floor near 2.5 MB/s. And the tree algorithms vary 10:1 across files, against mergedTL's 1.9:1, because a small alphabet such as ecoli's four letters lets a few deep trees shorten every scan.

Why the walk misses, and why runs help

An arbitrary permutation: every step lands somewhere new A run of equal bytes: each step lands next door Each cell is one table entry; arcs are successive steps of the walk. With a block much larger than the cache, the upper walk misses on almost every step. An illustration, not data. Through an arbitrary permutation each step lands somewhere new; through a run of equal bytes, as in kennedy, T points next door.

bzip2 itself decompresses bible at 67% of mergedTL's inversion rate, while also doing its Huffman and move-to-front decoding, so "no amount of re-engineering of bzip2 can increase its decompression speed much further". The paper ends on a caveat:

Such observations only hold true whilst cache sizes are much smaller than block sizes. Future growth in cache sizes may invalidate such findings.

items.title: 5. The same tradeoff, with four blocks live
items.text:
The K6-III's cache held 256 KB, against mergedTL's 4 MB for one block. Our workstation has a 20 MiB last-level cache, and a full bzip2 block, up to 900,000 rows at 4 bytes each, needs a 3.6 MB table. Read literally, the caveat has come true.

Two things kept Seward's sentence true anyway. A modern core keeps many misses in flight if it is given independent loads, so mibz2's walk advances 32 separate pieces of the chain in turn and runs 8.6 times as fast as one chain. And a decoder doesn't invert one block at a time. Four workers keep four tables live, 14.4 MB before any of their other buffers, in one cache they all share, and decoding with four costs more CPU time per byte than decoding with one: the workers finish sooner together, but compete for the memory system on the way. With the cache divided between blocks, caches are again much smaller than the tables being walked.

On Seward's axes a smaller table is a step down in speed. With four blocks sharing a cache, it also leaves more of the cache to the other three. Could the same links be stored in much less space, and would the lighter memory load make up for the extra work of reading a compressed entry? The first valid comparison answers both ways at once. The compact walk costs 14.85% more CPU time on one core and 15.95% less with four workers walking together. That result is about this traversal, measured on its own; what it means for the whole decoder is still open.

items.title: 6. A smaller table, a busier lookup
items.text:
The census of the navigation table found that most of its links follow simple patterns. An earlier format built on that, FOR-14, packed 14-bit offsets into fixed records. It halved the table, but extracting the packed bits made each step so much longer that the walk lost even with four workers, where it took 1.45 times as long as the ordinary walk.

Compact30 keeps each offset directly addressable instead. Its name means thirty rows per record, not thirty-bit pointers. A 64-byte record, aligned to a cache line, holds thirty 16-bit offsets and a 4-byte header. In an ordinary record the header carries a base position and the byte the thirty rows all output, and a row's next position is the base plus its offset. A group of rows that start with different bytes, or whose next positions are too far apart for 16-bit offsets, is stored instead as a RAW group: thirty full 4-byte entries, padded to 128 bytes.

One ordinary compact30 record

30 offsets, one per row30 × 2 bytes = 60 bytes H4 B Next position = the base in H + this row's offset H also holds the byte the record's rows output. Thirty rows in one cache line. RAW groups, segment starts and parking are handled outside this ordinary case.

On the measured corpus that brings the table from 4 bytes per row to 2.164, 45.9% less: about 1.95 MB for a full block instead of 3.6 MB, and 7.79 MB instead of 14.4 MB for four blocks at once.

Read against Seward's paper, the record combines three of its ideas. Its offsets rest on the ordering that makes \(T\) cheap to build: within one byte's bucket the links increase with the row, so a group's links are a base plus small offsets, smallest where the byte's occurrences in \(L\) sit close together, as in kennedy's runs. In Wikidata's blocks they usually do: about 77% of a full block's rows fall in 32-row groups that each come from a single run in \(L\). The header's byte is indexF's idea, emitting from \(F\) so that the walk needs no \(L\), with one byte stored per group in place of a search. And keeping the header and the offset in one cache line is mergedTL's. At 2.164 bytes a row, the record sits between treeopt-1M and indexF on Seward's memory axis, and aims at mergedTL's speed.

The step costs more, though. An ordinary compact30 step compiles to 21 instructions and four data loads; the conventional step is 16 instructions and three loads. Two of compact30's loads, the offset and the header, are both addressed from the current row, so neither waits for the other, but they are still two loads where the conventional step needs one. The walker's journal has the annotated disassembly.

So the question is which matters more when several cores share the machine: the extra instructions, or the smaller table.

items.title: 7. The four-worker reversal
items.text:
The comparison times two versions of the same traversal and assembly. The control walks mibz2's 4-byte table; compact30 walks its records with the same 32-lane walk. Every walk's output was checked byte for byte against the decoder's.

Only the walk is timed. Before each walk, the control builds its table with the decoder's own builder, while compact30 copies in records made beforehand by a reference builder, so the comparison measures how fast each prepared table is walked, not what it costs to build. The two preparations may also leave different data in cache.

The protocol used one corpus of 434 blocks (207 million rows) and 20 paired rounds, on one pinned core or four. With four, each worker prepared its next block, all four started walking together, and none checked its output until all had finished, with blocks dealt so that each worker had about the same number of rows. CPU cost is the threads' own CPU time, summed, per row. Completion time is the time from the first walk's start to the last walk's end in each step, summed over the steps. Neither is the decoder's elapsed time.

Conventional Compact30 Compact30 ÷ conventional (95% interval) CPU time per row, one core 1.221 ns 1.402 ns 1.148 (1.147–1.149) CPU time per row, four workers 2.055 ns 1.727 ns 0.840 (0.838–0.843) Completion time per pass, four workers 114.45 ms 97.97 ms 0.856 (0.852–0.860)

The intervals describe variation across the twenty rounds, on one machine and one corpus. Before the run, the protocol fixed what would justify building a direct constructor: the upper end of the four-worker CPU ratio at most 0.865, and of the completion ratio at most 1.02. The upper ends were 0.843 and 0.860. The analysis and an independent reconstruction from the individual walks agree on every figure.

CPU time per row, one core and four workers

The gain is spread across the workload. All 230 full-sized blocks were cheaper with compact30 at four workers, taking each block's average over the rounds, and compact30 used less CPU in 1,138 of the 1,140 full-sized four-worker steps. These are checks within one experiment, on blocks that repeat each round, not independent trials. The 204 short blocks were slower with compact30, but together they hold 8,324 rows, 0.004% of the total.

The run also had to show that the four walks started together, within 2% of each step's length. An earlier complete run failed that check, because waking sleeping workers delayed some walks by tens of microseconds, and it doesn't count. This run used a spinning start barrier instead, with nothing else changed; its worst start skew was 0.023%.

items.title: 8. Four workers cost the conventional walk far more
items.text:
From one core to four workers, the conventional walk's CPU cost per row rises from 1.221 ns to 2.055 ns, 68% more. Compact30's rises from 1.402 ns to 1.727 ns, 23% more. Both run under the same four-worker conditions, and the conventional table pays much more for them.

FOR-14 showed the same pattern earlier: from one block to four, the conventional walk's cost per row rose 56% and FOR-14's only 8%. Its smaller table removed most of the four-worker penalty, but each of its steps started 1.40 ns per row behind, three times what it saved. Compact30's step is cheap enough to come out ahead.

The obvious explanation is the table's size. Four conventional tables take about 14.4 MB, four compact30 tables about 7.79 MB, and the test machine's four cores share a 20 MiB last-level cache with everything else the workers use. Smaller tables could mean fewer evictions and less contention for memory, and they could also change address-translation costs.

Navigation tables for four full blocks

Conventional14.4 MB Compact307.79 MB One full-sized block per worker · table sizes, not cache occupancy The tables' sizes on the measured corpus. How much of each stays in cache, and how much memory traffic each causes, was not measured.

That explanation hasn't been tested. The run recorded no cache-miss or memory-controller counters, and the two arms prepared their tables differently before each walk, which by itself could change what is in cache when the walk starts. The size difference makes the cache explanation credible; it doesn't measure it.

The result also stops short of the decoder. A decoding worker doesn't spend all its time walking tables: it also reads input, reconstructs the last column, builds the table, assembles segments and writes output. Some of its walks run alone, and others overlap two or three neighbours rather than all four. So compact30's 14.85% loss on one core matters as much as its gain at four, and how much of a whole decode runs under four-way contention hasn't been measured.

items.title: 9. The table still has to be built
items.text:
The records in this comparison came from a reference builder that first computes every row's successor in a full-sized temporary array, then converts the result into compact30 records. That kept construction out of the measurement, but a decoder can't afford it. A direct builder has to produce the records from the block's last column and its byte counts, without the temporary array.

It also has to compete with the decoder's current builder, which places every row in one counting-sort pass and writes runs of sixteen equal bytes sixteen entries at a time. Compact30's builder has to write group headers, check offsets against the 16-bit limit, and move groups to RAW, and still stay close to that.

The traversal result sets the budget. A rough planning model puts the decoder's current table building at 0.592 CPU-seconds per decoded GB, and the traversal with its assembly at 1.847. If b and w are compact30's building and traversal costs as fractions of today's, the saving is about 0.592 × (1 − b) + 1.847 × (1 − w) CPU-seconds per GB, and the target is at least 0.25.

If the four-worker traversal ratio carried over to the decoder, a builder costing the same as today's would save about 0.295 CPU-seconds per GB. The builder could be up to 7.5% slower than today's at the central estimate, or 6.7% using the conservative end of the interval. That is a budget conditional on the traversal gain surviving inside the decoder, built on approximate phase costs; meeting it would justify the next test, not settle the question.

The next step is a design for that builder, set out in the constructor brief. Its main difficulty is already clear. Groups that straddle two bytes' rows can be found from the byte counts before any row is placed, but a group whose offsets turn out too wide is only known when its last row lands, and has to move to RAW then. The builder has to produce exactly the records tested here, and the first measurements will be whether it does and what it costs. After that, a whole-decoder comparison can show how much of the four-worker gain survives in practice.

For now, a smaller navigation table has beaten the conventional one in a controlled four-worker traversal while losing on a single core. That is a strong reason to study the memory contention behind it, and a concrete budget for building the table.

items.title: Concepts
items.text:
mibz2 decodes bzip2 as libbzip2 1.0.8 defines it, byte for byte, with every check libbzip2 makes, and decodes several blocks at once.

  • Why 32 couriers beat one: memory-level parallelism, the decoder's premise. One courier waits at every stop to learn the next address; 32 couriers' waits overlap. The lanes, the prefetch, the per-step cost that binds next, and the measurements.
  • What is checked, and when: block CRCs, stream CRCs, what an error reports, and the four inputs mibz2 refuses where libbzip2 does not.
  • How it works: the one sequential phase (the scanner), the workers, and the inverse BWT walked as 32 interleaved chains.
  • Prior work: libbzip2; Kärkkäinen, Kempa and Puglisi (DCC 2012); lbzip2 and pbzip2.

items.title: Block CRCs, before the block's bytes
items.text: Every block's CRC is checked before any of that block's bytes are returned. A block whose CRC does not match returns none of its bytes: the error comes instead. The bytes returned before an error are exactly the stream's up to the bad block.

items.title: Stream CRCs, at the stream's end
items.text:
Each stream's combined CRC is checked at the stream's end. The bytes of a stream's blocks are returned as each block is verified, before the stream's own CRC has been read. So a streaming caller has the whole stream verified only once a read reaches its end without an error: until then, what it has read is provisional.

In Python, BZ2Reader.verified turns true only when a read returns the end with every block's and stream's CRC matched.

items.title: Where an error was found
items.text:
An error says where decoding failed: in Rust Error { kind, block, bit }, in Python the DecodeError message. That is which block, and the bit it starts at. A damaged bit can be found later than where it lies, since the input is only known to be wrong once something it encodes fails a check.

The error kinds (ErrorKind):

  • the input: Empty, NotBz2, Truncated, TrailingData;
  • each of libbzip2's block checks: BadBlockMagic, BadOrigPtr, NoSymbols, BadGroups, BadSelectors, BadSelector, BadCodeLength, BadHuffmanCode, SelectorOverrun, RunTooLong, BlockTooLong, RunUnfinished;
  • BlockCrc and StreamCrc, with the stored and computed values;
  • this decoder's refusals: Randomised, BlockTooLarge;
  • Io (from a BzReader's source), RangeOvershoot, Cancelled, and Internal (a caught panic: a bug).

items.title: What is decoded, and what is refused
items.text:
The format is libbzip2 1.0.8's, with every check it makes: bzip2 1.0 and later output. Four choices differ from it, and each has its own error:

input libbzip2 mibz2 randomised blocks (written only by bzip2 0.9.0 and earlier, before 1999) decoded refused (Randomised) bytes after the last stream that do not begin another stream ignored an error (TrailingData): nothing after a stream is silently dropped an oversubscribed Huffman code pointing past the alphabet a stale table entry read an error a block whose compressed form passes 64 MiB (a real block is at most about 4.2 MB) decoded an error (BlockTooLarge)

items.title: Why 32 couriers beat one: understanding memory-level parallelism
items.text:
Most of a bzip2 decode is one loop, the inverse Burrows–Wheeler transform's walk, and that loop spends most of its time waiting for memory. mibz2 doesn't make memory any faster. It keeps many of the walk's memory requests in flight at once, so the waits overlap. That is memory-level parallelism (MLP), and it is the library's basic premise.

This page explains it with couriers and a dispatcher, then gives the mechanism behind each part of the picture, and the measurements so far. How it works has the threads around the walk, and Prior work the work it builds on.

items.title: One courier, one chain
items.text:
A motorcycle courier learns each delivery address only on arriving at the previous one: open the envelope, read the next address. The third destination can't be known before reaching the second. The bike is fast, but most of the time goes on waiting to find out where to go next.

That is the ordinary inverse BWT:

  • The table. After Huffman decoding and move-to-front, a block's last column becomes the T-vector: one 32-bit entry a row, holding the row's byte (bits 0–7) and the next row (the bits above). A block holds up to 900,000 bytes, so the table is up to 3.6 MB, larger than most cores' L2 cache.
  • The walk. Start at the block's primary index. Each step loads the current row's entry, writes its byte, and takes the next row from the same entry. The next row is anywhere in the table, so the load usually misses the cache.
  • The wait. The step after can't start until that load returns, because its address is in the load's result. A chain of dependent loads keeps one miss in flight, and the core idles through each one.
courier 1the corewaiting for the next address (a cache miss)idle: nothing to do until the address comes backa steptime → One courier. Each step (dark) is a few instructions; most of the time goes on waiting for the next address (light). Schematic, not to scale.

The walk was measured as latency-bound directly, on the machine where mibz2's prototype was built: walking 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 independent chains through one block, the cost fell from 28.5 to 4.4 cycles a byte of output (compute frontier, section 2). Memory bandwidth was nowhere near its limit. The walk was waiting, not moving data. libbzip2 and lbzip2 walk the one chain.

items.title: 32 couriers, 32 independent journeys
items.text:
Give each of 32 couriers a different delivery chain. While courier 1 waits for its next address, couriers 2, 3, 4… make progress. That is memory-level parallelism: the couriers don't travel faster, but there are enough independent journeys that waiting on one doesn't stop the rest. One courier is limited by the time it takes to get each new address; 32 keep many requests in flight.

courier 1courier 2courier 3courier 4the coreslots for couriers 5 to 32each courier's step, one after anothertime → Four of mibz2's 32 couriers. Each still waits as long for its address, but the waits overlap, and the core takes the other couriers' steps in the gaps. Schematic, not to scale.

The correction that keeps the picture faithful

The CPU doesn't employ 32 workers, and the lanes aren't threads. One core interleaves the instructions of 32 traversal chains, and its out-of-order machinery overlaps their memory requests. The better image is one dispatch centre managing 32 motorcycles, each getting its next destination only when its last delivery returns an address.

What counts is deliveries a second for the whole centre, not how fast one bike finishes its route: sustained throughput, not the latency of any one load. Every load still takes as long as before.

Several threads are several dispatch centres, one a block: mibz2's workers decode whole blocks in parallel (How it works). The lanes are the parallelism inside each one.

items.title: Where the independent journeys come from
items.text:
A block has one chain, not 32: the T-vector is a single cycle through every row (or, for a periodic text, a few). bzip2 carries no metadata to start a walk anywhere but the primary index. mibz2 makes the journeys itself:

  • Random starts. 511 pseudo-random rows, plus the walk's own first row, become segment starts. A random row is a random position in the text, so the cycle is cut into 512 segments of about equal length. (Evenly spaced rows clustered in the text and stalled the lanes.)
  • Flagged starts end a segment. Each start is flagged in bit 31 of its own T-vector entry, which links never use. A lane that reads a flagged entry has run into the next segment's start: its segment ends there, recording which start it ran into, and the lane takes the next unwalked segment.
  • 32 lanes walk in lockstep. Each round, every lane takes one step, writing its byte into its own segment's buffer.
  • The segments are stitched together afterwards. From the first row's segment, each segment is followed by the one it ran into, until the block's length is reached. The output is exactly the plain walk's, byte for byte, including a periodic block's several cycles. The flags are cleared before the walk returns.
  • Short blocks walk plainly. Under 64 KiB, the segments' bookkeeping costs more than the waits it hides; only a stream's last block is ever that short.
one chaincut at startsjoinedthe plain walk: one courier, row after row, from the primary index to the block's endA · lane 1B · lane 3C · lane 2D · lane 4E · lane 2F · lane 1G · lane 4H · lane 3▼ a start row, flagged in its own entry: the segment before it ends there, and a lane takes the nextA, then the segment A ran into (B), then C… until the block's length: exactly the plain walk's bytes One chain cut at flagged starts into segments, walked by four lanes in whatever order the lanes take them, then joined in order. mibz2 cuts each block into 512 segments for 32 lanes.

items.title: Prefetching: phoning ahead
items.text:
Lanes alone weren't enough. Without help, a lane's next load is issued only when its instructions enter the core's reorder buffer, which is full of the other lanes' steps. So the misses in flight were bounded by how many steps that window holds, and adding lanes didn't add misses.

mibz2 issues a software prefetch of each lane's next entry as soon as its row is known (prefetcht0 on x86-64, prfm pldl1keep on aarch64). A prefetch retires without waiting for its data, so every lane's miss starts at once. In the picture, the dispatcher phones each request through the moment an address is read, rather than when that courier's turn comes round on the board.

Try the counts yourself in this schematic. It has one dispatcher, whose paperwork for a step takes a tick or two, and each address takes 31 ticks to come back. The timings are made up for the picture.

The schematic needs JavaScript.

items.title: The dispatcher becomes the bottleneck
items.text:
There is only so much road, and one dispatcher. Add enough couriers and every wait is covered. Then the limit is the dispatcher: each step's paperwork, done for each courier in turn. Add more couriers past that point and the dispatcher spends more on coordination than the extra journeys earn.

In the core, the dispatcher's limits are these:

  • Instructions a step. Every lane's step is a handful of instructions: the load, the flag test, the byte's store, the write pointer's advance, the buffer-end check, the prefetch. With the misses overlapped, the walk runs at the rate the core can issue those instructions.
  • Register pressure. One lane's state (its row, its write pointers, its segment) fits in registers, but 32 lanes' state doesn't. It lives in the L1 cache, and every step loads and stores some of it.
  • Cache contention. The lanes' table lines, the 512 segments' buffers and the lanes' own state share the same caches. At four threads, four walks share the L3.
  • Outstanding misses. A core tracks only so many misses at once (its line fill buffers, and the L2's own queue). Beyond that, more lanes only queue.

The record shows both sides. Without the prefetch, 16 lanes were within noise of 12, and 24 or 32 were slower (PR #21). With it, 16 to 32 lanes were about 26–28% faster than 12 lanes without it, and within noise of each other at one walk. With four walks at once, 32 lanes won clearly. So mibz2 runs 32 lanes and 512 segments (the measured points).

It also explains why a cleverer-looking algorithm can lose. Once 32 misses are in flight, the walk is bound by instructions a step, not by the latency of each load. A change that saves steps but makes each one dearer loses. A change that keeps the steps and makes them cheaper wins.

items.title: Make the dispatcher efficient
items.text:
Once there are enough couriers, cut the paperwork a step. That's how the walk got faster:

  • The flagged walk (#12). It replaced the first segmented walk, which tested every step's row against a separate bitmap of the starts (12 lanes, 256 segments). The flag moved into the entry the step loads anyway, bytes went out through raw per-lane pointers instead of a growable vector's push, and the test for idle lanes left the hot loop.
  • The prefetch, with 32 lanes and 512 segments (#21): every lane's next miss starts at once, as above.
  • The shared-offset walk, after libsais's chain decode (#37, the default walk since 0.1.5). libsais 2.12's decode_chains runs room rounds of every chain at a shared output offset, where room is the fewest bytes any chain's buffer has spare. Within a pass, a lane's byte goes to its buffer's base plus the pass's offset, so the per-step pointer store and buffer-end test are gone. The lanes, the prefetch and the segments are unchanged, so the same misses are in flight. Only the instructions a step drop: one dispatcher's paperwork, done in batches.

Two cleverer-looking ideas from the literature were built, measured and dropped. Both changed the journeys themselves, and both lost to their extra cost a step:

  • The pair walk, ψ² (#34, after libsais and Kärkkäinen, Kempa and Puglisi's super-alphabet). Each entry holds the row two steps on, so the walk takes half the steps, two bytes at each. But each step costs about twice as much: the second byte comes from a first-byte lookup. With the prefetch keeping 32 misses in flight, halving the dependent loads bought almost nothing, and the pair table took about three times as long to build. Envelopes holding two addresses mean fewer stops, but twice the paperwork at each, and the envelopes take three times as long to fill.
  • Precopy (#36, after Kärkkäinen and Puglisi). Where a stretch of the walk repeats one already walked, its bytes are copied instead of walked. It copied 31.5% of the Wikidata blocks' bytes, and was slower all the same. The repeat check ran on every step, and the steps it skipped were the cheap ones, whose table lines were already in cache. The cost is in the scattered steps, which repeats never cover. A courier who checks the logbook for a repeated stretch at every stop loses more time than the short, nearby stretches it saves.
flagged walk (the default before #37): a step's journey, then its bookkeepingshared-offset walk (#37, the default): the same journeys, less bookkeeping a steppair walk, ψ² (#34, lost): two bytes a step, about twice the work a stepPrecopy (#36, lost): a repeat check on every step; the copies skip only cheap stepsthe journey: load the entry, take its bytebookkeeping: flags, pointers, buffer ends, checksa byte out The core's time once enough misses are in flight, schematically: the bytes out in the same time. The shared-offset walk keeps the journeys and cuts the bookkeeping. The pair walk halves the steps but doubles each one's work, and pays again in its build. Precopy adds a check to every step to skip a few cheap ones.

items.title: The picture, term by term
items.text: in the picture in the decoder a courier a lane: one traversal chain, walking one segment at a time a delivery address, read on arrival the next row, in the entry the step just loaded waiting for the address a cache miss on the T-vector a delivery chain a segment, from a flagged start row to the next start the dispatcher one core's instruction stream, interleaving all the lanes' steps the paperwork for each step the instructions a step: the flag test, the byte's store, the pointer and buffer bookkeeping phoning ahead the software prefetch of each lane's next entry the road, the board's size the core's limits: outstanding misses (line fill buffers), the reorder window, the caches deliveries a second for the centre bytes of output a second: throughput, not one load's latency several dispatch centres worker threads, one block each

items.title: Threads
items.text:
• The scanner. One thread reads each block's header and Huffman-coded symbols in order. This is the one sequential phase: a block's end is known only once its symbols are read. It finds blocks exactly, not by searching for the block magic, so a magic inside a block's data is never taken for a block. It is roughly a tenth of a decode on well-compressed text, more on poorly compressible data.
  • The workers. Each worker finishes a block: move-to-front, the T-vector, the inverse BWT walk, RLE1 and the CRC.
  • The reader takes the blocks in order. A block's error reaches the reader only once every block before it has been read.
  • Memory is bounded: at most slots blocks are in flight (by default twice the threads), and the buffers are reused from block to block.

With one thread, the same phases run in order on the calling thread.

items.title: The walk
items.text:
The inverse BWT is a chain of dependent loads: each step's row is the previous step's load. A plain walk keeps one load in flight. The default walk (bwt::walk_segments_room, the flagged walk in passes) keeps many, one a lane (Why 32 couriers beat one explains why, and where it stops paying):

  • 512 pseudo-random rows, the walk's first among them, are segment starts;
  • each start is flagged in its own T-vector entry, which ends the segment before it;
  • 32 lanes walk segments in lockstep, each taking the next segment when its own ends, and each lane's next entry is prefetched as soon as its row is known;
  • the lanes step in passes of room rounds, room the fewest bytes any lane's buffer has spare, each byte written at its lane's base plus the pass's offset, so a step has no pointer store or buffer-end test (after libsais's chain decode, #37);
  • the segments are joined in order.

It equals the plain walk on every list, lists of several cycles included: the join follows the segments' links until the block's length is reached. The flags are cleared before the walk returns. Blocks under 64 Ki are walked plainly. The kernel is behind bwt::InverseBwt (Segmented, the default; Plain), so a walk can be swapped and timed as part of the whole decoder.

items.title: Kernels
items.text: Kernels::detect() chooses at run time: AVX2 (with BMI1) for move-to-front and RLE1, and PCLMULQDQ for the CRC. Each has a scalar twin, used on any other CPU and on aarch64 (Kernels::scalar()). The walk's gain is scalar code, memory-level parallelism, so it holds on any CPU.

items.title: Prior work
items.text:
• The format and its checks are libbzip2's (Julian Seward, bzip2 1.0.8, decompress.c). mibz2 follows its decoding rules and makes each of its checks, in its terms. Its Huffman decode tables are built as BZ2_hbCreateDecodeTables builds them, so a stream libbzip2 refuses is refused here too. It is a separate implementation in Rust, not a port of libbzip2's code. The tests use libbzip2 itself (the bzip2 crate's bundled 1.0.8) as the oracle.
  • Interleaving several traversals of one BWT inversion on one thread, so that out-of-order execution keeps their loads in flight, is Kärkkäinen, Kempa and Puglisi's idea: "Slashing the Time for BWT Inversion", DCC 2012, pp. 99–108.
    • They also use a super-alphabet (an LF² table: two characters a dependent lookup) and "Precopy" for repetitive data. Neither is used here: both were built in mibz2 and lost (why).
    • What is particular here is only how the traversals are found in an existing bzip2 file, which carries no metadata for them: the random starts, the flagged starts that end each segment, and the joining in order.
  • libsais (Ilya Grebnov), 2.12's cyclic inverse BWT, "as used by bzip2": its RUN_LANES store, 16 equal last-column bytes linked at once, is in mibz2's T-vector build. Its chain decode's shared-offset passes are mibz2's walk since 0.1.5 (#37).
  • Block-parallel decoding is lbzip2's (Mikołaj Izdebski) and pbzip2's approach.
  • pbz2 (Soof Golan) arrived independently at a segmented, multi-chain walk too; the bake-off that found it is in the journals.

items.title: Python
items.text:
mibz2 needs Python 3.10 or later. It has no Python dependencies.

pip install mibz2

or with uv:

uv add mibz2

Wheels are built for Linux (x86-64, aarch64), macOS (x86-64, arm64) and Windows (x64). Each uses the stable ABI (abi3), so one wheel covers every Python version from 3.10.

items.title: Rust
items.text:
cargo add mibz2

The library depends on std only. Its minimum supported Rust version is 1.80. The python feature builds the Python extension module, and is only for maturin.

items.title: Python
items.text:
Write a .bz2 file with the standard library's bz2, to have one to read:

import bz2

with bz2.open("sample.bz2", "wb") as f:
    for i in range(10_000):
        f.write(f"line {i}\n".encode())

A whole file in memory, decoded on every CPU this process may use, or on one thread:

>>> import mibz2
>>> compressed = open("sample.bz2", "rb").read()
>>> data = mibz2.decompress(compressed)
>>> data == bz2.decompress(compressed)
True
>>> mibz2.decompress(compressed, threads=1) == data
True

A file read as it is decoded: open takes a path or a binary file object, and returns a buffered binary file. Its raw.verified turns true once a read has reached the end with every block's and stream's CRC matched:

>>> with mibz2.open("sample.bz2") as f:
...     first = f.readline()
...     before = f.raw.verified
...     rest = f.read()
...     after = f.raw.verified
>>> first, before, after
(b'line 0\n', False, True)

A bad input raises mibz2.DecodeError, a ValueError, from decompress or from the read at which it is found. The message says which block and bit decoding failed at:

>>> damaged = bytearray(compressed)
>>> damaged[len(damaged) // 2] ^= 0x10
>>> try:
...     mibz2.decompress(bytes(damaged))
... except mibz2.DecodeError as e:
...     print(type(e).__name__, isinstance(e, ValueError))
DecodeError True

items.title: Rust
items.text:
use std::io::Read;

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    // a whole .bz2 in memory (its streams one after another): on this thread, or on 4
    let data = std::fs::read("file.bz2")?;
    let text = mibz2::decode(&data)?;
    let same = mibz2::decode_parallel(&data, 4)?;
    assert_eq!(text, same);

    // any Read, as a Read: on this thread, or block-parallel on 4 worker threads
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    mibz2::BzReader::parallel(std::fs::File::open("file.bz2")?, 4).read_to_end(&mut out)?;
    Ok(())
}

A bad stream is an mibz2::Error (its kind, block and bit), or from a BzReader an io::Error of kind InvalidData wrapping it. The Rust reference lists the rest: the push decoder, the block scanner and the decoding of a range of blocks.
